main_thread.title: The Missing Core
main_thread.description: Work out what the Ninth-Hand actually is, what was taken out of it, and why the thing inside it registered you rather than anyone else. Keep the Board licensed, the Ossuary uninterested, and TRACE low enough to survive - while steadily raising every other figure, because the alternative is dying poor in a belt full of people who would strip your hull before your body cooled. The vessel never shows you a plan of itself - it tells you one need at a time, a node or a section or a part, and it has never once asked for the core.
main_thread.plot_notes: Three acts. Act 1 is hiding the ship; Act 2 is the ship getting too loud to hide and the Garland starting to take an interest in it; Act 3 is the empty seat. Each act should open up further physical reach as REACH climbs and should tighten the consequences of TRACE. The central question is never answered cleanly and never early: what the core was, where it went, and what the protagonist is being used as in its absence. Descant is present in the overwhelming majority of scenes and its regard for the protagonist should move as much as any human's.

acts.title: Dead Weight
acts.description: Eleven years of scraping by, and now a corridor behind a bulkhead that should have been solid. Keep working the belt, keep the licence current, and start finding out what you have been living inside. Nothing about the Ninth-Hand can be explained to anyone yet, including yourself.
completion_signals: The System has issued and the operator has completed at least one genuine directive, at a cost actually paid on the page
At least one other person has noticed that the Ninth-Hand is running better than its papers say
The operator has learned enough to know that the sheet Descant keeps for them is not the whole sheet

acts.title: Better Than Its Papers
acts.description: The Ninth-Hand can speak now, and it can travel, and neither can be hidden for long. Tally Station has opinions. A buyer pays too well, an archivist pays for things that weigh nothing, and a diver who never gets hurt starts turning up in the same wrecks. The ship reacts to some people and not to others, and will not say why. The hours the operator loses stop being small enough to call fatigue. If the ship gets loud enough, the Meridian Ossuary sends someone polite with a warrant.
completion_signals: Lark Ferris has been inside the vessel's true interior and the operator has seen the ship respond to them
The Threnody Index has bought something the operator knows and given something true back
Someone beyond the Garland crews - the Board, the Ossuary, or a buyer with no name - has taken a direct interest in the Ninth-Hand
The operator has seen the Index's lineage record and knows where it ends

acts.title: Tacet
acts.description: The core was never an object, and the vessel has finally said what it has needed all along. A seat is empty at the heart of the ship, and something will be done about it. The operator can sit in it, can let someone else sit in it, or can refuse both and let the ship go back to being silent - and every one of those costs a person. The choice does not wait: a ship with no core cannot outrun the next warrant, and somewhere in the belt a stretch of debris has stopped tumbling. The choice is the operator's own: no one, the ship included, is allowed to make it for him.
completion_signals: The System has asked, in its own voice, for the seat to be filled
The operator has told Lark what the Index record says, or has decided not to, and that decision has been on the page
Someone has sat in the seat, or the operator has refused it for good

subplot_001.title: The Standing Orders
subplot_001.description: Descant does not show the operator a ship. It surfaces one need at a time - current for a node, air for a section, a Consonance part it cannot fabricate on its own - and never explains how the pieces fit until they already have. It has never once put the core on that list.
subplot_001.ties_to_main_plot: Every order answered is one more thing the vessel doesn't need the operator's body for - except the one thing it never asks for.

subplot_002.title: Third Class, Six Weeks
subplot_002.description: The salvage licence expires in six weeks and renewal requires a Board survey of the hull - a survey that would put an inspector inside the Ninth-Hand with instruments. Let it lapse and there is no appeal: an unlicensed hull in the Garland is salvage itself, and the Board impounds it.
subplot_002.ties_to_main_plot: The first hard deadline, and the first time hiding the ship costs real money or real trouble - and the first paper anyone holds on it. Lose the licence and the Board impounds the Ninth-Hand.
subplot_002._fail_when_note: Deadline made deterministic at turn 155 (editor's call; first set at 100, pushed back so the licence does not end the story before the other destinations can be reached): the licence lapses when the Board says so (flag licence_lapsed) or, failing that, at turn 155. A thread already completed is never failed. Failure makes ending_4 ready_when true, and the funnel can commit from open_until (80) at each 10-turn check, so a player who has not resolved this thread by 155 is committed to Salvage Rights at the turn-160 check, at the very end of the narrow phase (narrow_until 160). The turn count is under story_clock (built): up to 3 idle turns in a row do not count, so 155 is a floor on real turns played, not an exact turn.

subplot_003.title: A Second Pair of Hands
subplot_003.description: The work is beyond one person and has been for years. Finding somebody you would trust aboard is difficult; finding somebody the System will register is a different problem entirely.
subplot_003.ties_to_main_plot: The vessel has opinions about who comes inside it, and those opinions are the clearest window into what it thinks the protagonist is for.

subplot_004.title: What Tally Remembers
subplot_004.description: Somebody at Tally Station has been buying non-inert Consonance parts for years, quietly, and paying far too well for them.
subplot_004.ties_to_main_plot: The first thread leading anywhere near what was taken out of the ship - and it fails if the Ninth-Hand gets loud enough for the Ossuary to reach the buyer first.

subplot_005.title: The Diver
subplot_005.description: Lark Ferris works the wrecks nobody else will and walks out of them every time. Get close enough to find out whether that is skill, and find out what it costs to be let close.
subplot_005.ties_to_main_plot: The one person in the Garland the vessel reacts to, and the operator cannot tell whether that is jealousy or recognition.

subplot_006.title: Four Hundred Years Wrong
subplot_006.description: The Threnody Index's factor at Tally pays for what the operator knows rather than what they haul - a script nobody taught them, the hours they lose, the tune under the carrier. Every answer sold buys a question back. The Index has been failing to explain the Fall for four hundred years; its oldest project turns out to be something else.
subplot_006.ties_to_main_plot: The only road to where the core went - and the price of the road is telling a faction exactly what the operator is.

subplot_007.title: The Empty Seat
subplot_007.description: For the whole of its restoration the vessel has asked for one thing at a time and never once asked for the core. Now it does. Descant names the seat, says what it is for, and asks - not orders - for it to be filled. It will not choose who. It has a preference, and it knows the operator can hear it.
subplot_007.ties_to_main_plot: The question the whole story has been avoiding, asked by the one voice that has known the answer from the first day.

subplot_008.title: Requisition
subplot_008.description: The Meridian Ossuary does not buy. Once the Ninth-Hand is loud enough to have a file, an Assessor comes to the Garland with a warrant that every port must honour, and starts asking polite questions. A requisition cannot be argued with. It can be outrun, buried under a cleaner-looking hull, or bought off by giving him something else live - and every one of those costs the ship something it will not get back.
subplot_008.ties_to_main_plot: The world's answer to TRACE. It turns hiding the ship from a habit into a price, and in the last act it is the clock on the empty seat: a ship with no core cannot outrun the next warrant.

subplot_009.title: The Quiet Stretch
subplot_009.description: Somewhere in the deep belt the debris has stopped tumbling. A crew the operator knows went in there three days ago and their beacon is still calling. They are all aboard, uninjured, sitting down together in their galley with the meal half-eaten; the log stops at the midpoint of a word. Nothing did this that anyone can point at. For the first time since the bulkhead, the page behind the operator's eyes goes blank of its own accord, and stays blank until they are well clear. If the operator came to the belt after a crew that did not come back, this is the second time he has seen this, and he knows it before anyone says it.
subplot_009.ties_to_main_plot: The one time the story lets the thing that ended the Consonance come close enough to feel, and the moment the operator learns why a ship would choose to be silent for four thousand years.

subplot_010.title: What Followed You Here
subplot_010.description: The ship is getting louder, and whatever the operator came to the Garland to get away from has heard it. Read 'Came to the belt after' on the PLAYER line and play only the matching branch. DEBT: Dace Orrin has bought the note, and is friendly, patient and legally entitled to the Ninth-Hand as collateral. The only thing aboard worth enough to clear it is something live, and selling one either brings the Ossuary or strips the ship. WARRANT: Oren Thale's filing has matched the operator's face to an old open warrant in a system he will not name. Thale offers to lose it, which makes the operator useful to the Ossuary for exactly as long as Thale likes. What the operator actually did is settled on the page the first time anyone asks, and never changes afterwards. LOSS: Hesper Vaunt has bought a beacon log from the system the operator came from, and it is his old crew's. The last minutes are all of them sitting down together in the galley, talking less and less, and the final entry stops at the midpoint of a word.
subplot_010.ties_to_main_plot: Whatever he ran from is what made him somebody nobody would come looking for - and so somebody the ship could choose. Now somebody has come looking, and the price of making them go away is always paid in the ship.

subplot_011.title: Off Shift
subplot_011.description: Between dives there is the rest of it: drinks at Tally that run late, a shared meal eaten standing at a manifold, the slow business of two people who have both worked alone for years finding out what it is like not to. What grows between the operator and Lark is built out of work done together and things said honestly, and it moves at her pace as much as his - she has kept people at arm's length for nine years and does not stop on anyone's schedule. It can become physical. If it does, it is because both of them chose it in the scene, out loud or unmistakably; either of them can say not yet or no, and that is honoured on the page. Aboard the Ninth-Hand nothing is private - the ship is the only witness to everything - so the first time is likelier to happen somewhere else: a rented room above a Tally bar, or the cramped bunk of Lark's own cutter.
subplot_011.ties_to_main_plot: The more she means to him, the more every ending costs. Handing her the seat, sitting in it himself, and refusing both are all decisions about her - and the ship has been watching the two of them the whole time.

subplot_012._authored: Texture: carries nothing, never touches an ending. Opens early (act 1) once the story has had a few turns to breathe. Medium priority on purpose: the pacing nudge names only the top thread and the next two by title, so a low-priority texture would never be seen behind the spine threads. No ties_to_main_plot, deliberately. The text never says 'Descant' (not available below QUORUM 40). Also waits while subplot_016 (Four Kinds of Attention) is live.
subplot_012.title: A Day Rate
subplot_012.description: Another crew, two hulks over, is a cutter short and pays by the day: help lift one awkward frame section before it drifts out of reach. The work is undignified and the crew are good company - they rib, understate, and tell the same bad story twice. Something goes wrong in the hands: a plate that will not stay where it is put, a share of the take smaller than the handshake. It is done when the section is on the tally and everyone has been paid, or has agreed not to bring it up.

subplot_013._authored: Texture: carries nothing, never touches an ending. Starts only after 'A Day Rate' closes and not before turn 20, so at most one texture thread is live (the engine does not enforce that for authored threads). The failing system is deliberately NOT the hull, so the fix is not priced as a FRAME repair, and not a Consonance system, so it does not read as QUORUM or SYNC business. Also waits while subplot_015 (Moving Day, act 3) is live.
subplot_013.title: The Reclaimer, Again
subplot_013.description: Something small and unglamorous aboard is giving out - the water reclaimer, most likely, or the galley stove - in a way that makes every other job worse. Nothing about it is mysterious: the ship has simply been patched past its patience. The System reports each failure in the same flat voice it uses for everything else. Fix it with what is aboard, badly, and live with how it smells afterwards.

subplot_014._authored: Texture: carries nothing, never touches an ending. Set at Tally, so it waits for REACH 20 (the tally_reach gate) as well as the previous texture closing. Uses faction_crews' 'bound by favours rather than contracts'. Kept off the named cast: Lark, Hesper, Oren and Dace each carry plot, and a texture thread should not spend them. Also waits while subplot_015 (Moving Day, act 3) is live.
subplot_014.title: Claim Jumped
subplot_014.description: At Tally, two crews are each certain they cut the same wreck first, and each has a favour it means to call in. The operator was out there when it happened, and neither side has thought to ask what they saw until now. Nobody wants a fight; they want a witness, a story that lets them keep face, and a drink bought by somebody else. Whoever the operator sides with owes them one, and the other crew remembers.

subplot_015._authored: Texture: carries nothing, never touches an ending. The Act 3 breather, set against the seat: the choice costs a person, and this is a small ordinary favour for someone who is leaving the belt with nothing lost. A goodbye disguised as a chore, so it echoes the exit shape in world.rules without being a crew exit (the leaver is a colleague, not a tracked relationship). Opens on act 3 only when no earlier texture is live (subplot_013 and subplot_014 carry the reverse guard), because the engine does not enforce one-texture-at-a-time for authored threads. Deliberately independent of the chain, so a player who never finished it still gets one. Kept off Tally by name, since REACH 20 is not guaranteed. The text never says 'Descant'.
subplot_015.title: Moving Day
subplot_015.description: A fellow salvager the operator has worked beside for years is quitting the belt for good, and the Ninth-Hand is the only ship in reach with the hold for everything they own. The job is furniture, a stove that will not go through the lock, a cat with views about vacuum, and strong opinions on how it should be packed. It is a goodbye disguised as a chore; both of them know it and neither says so. It is done when the last of it is stowed, delivered, or left where it will do the most good.

subplot_016._authored: Texture: carries nothing, never touches an ending. Puts all four factions on the page early, through one ordinary morning of dealing with each of them, so their goals (world.factions.*.goals, sent to the narrator every turn as flat description) land as something the operator has actually seen before the spine threads put weight on them (Third Class = the Board, Requisition = the Ossuary, What Tally Remembers = the Index via Hesper, Claim Jumped = the Crews). Dramatised, not stated: the Board is a weigh-clerk and a form, the Crews are a favour with no paper behind it, the Index pays for a story rather than a part, the Ossuary is a rumour about a hold that changed hands with no sale. No named cast - the clerk, the crew, the scout are anonymous, so Lark, Hesper, Oren and Dace stay unspent for their own threads. Deliberately not set at Tally (REACH 20 is not guaranteed this early for two of the three starting classes); the depot and the Garland are enough. Opens at turn 3, well ahead of subplot_012 (turn 6), and subplot_012 guards against it being active - since 'completed' never reverts, that one guard is enough to keep every later texture thread clear of it too.
subplot_016.title: Four Kinds of Attention
subplot_016.description: A morning of nothing but paperwork puts every power in the Garland in front of the operator, none of it about him personally. The Board's weigh-clerk totals the hold to the gram and initials a form that records exactly what was found and nothing about what it might be. A Garland crew calls in an old favour over nothing grander than a spare coupling - the kind of debt nobody writes down and nobody forgets. A Threnody Index scout offers real money for a story rather than a part, and does not flinch when the story is thin. And word goes round the depot, secondhand and already worn smooth, that the Ossuary took a rival's hold down the row without paying for it, and that crew has stopped bringing it up. Nobody asks the operator's opinion of any of this. That is worth noticing.

story_clock.push_directive: The Ninth-Hand's channel lights with a Reclamation Board notice, stamped ahead of schedule: whatever the operator has been putting off, the belt has just made a date for it. Let it arrive as something concrete - a message, a hail, a person at the lock - that needs an answer now, and let the operator's next choice be about that.

initial_scene.summary: The operator has just cut open a bulkhead in their own ship's aft hold, chasing a failed coolant line, and found a clean, warm corridor behind it that is longer than the hull it sits in. Something back there has registered them as its operator and put four figures behind their eyes for the first time in eleven years.

opening_scene.narration_before_name:
Eleven years you have flown the Ninth-Hand, and eleven years it has been dying, and you are the only reason it has not finished. You know it by sound. The reactor's flutter on cold start. The hold door that needs a hip. The particular scream the aft coolant line makes about ninety seconds before it goes.

Tonight it does not scream. It just stops, and the hold goes over-warm, and you take the cutter to the bulkhead behind the line because there is nothing back there but foam and forty years of somebody else's bad repairs.

There is no foam. There is no conduit, no rust, no bad repair. The cut opens onto a corridor - unlit but not dark, the surfaces pale and seamless and perfectly clean - and it runs aft. It runs much further aft than your ship is long. You stand there with the cutter still hot in your hand and do the arithmetic three times and it does not work any of the three.

Something in there turns on. Not lights. Attention. It settles over you the way a hand settles on the back of a neck. And it is not new. That is the part that gets into you - it is not new at all, it is a weight you have carried so long you had stopped calling it anything.

Then something opens behind your eyes. Not a voice - a page, laid over the hold, in a script you were never taught and read perfectly anyway.

[Operator detected.]

[Designation required.]

It does not ask. There is nothing in it that could ask. It states the gap, and waits for you to fill it.
opening_scene.narration_after_name:
[{player_name}. Recorded.]

Nothing else. No greeting, no explanation, no acknowledgement that anything has occurred. Five figures arrive beneath the words, unlabelled in any language you were taught and legible anyway. Four are low. One is lower than all of them, and it is the one you cannot find a meaning for.

You stand in the warm dark with the cutter cooling in your hand and ask the obvious thing out loud, because there is nobody here to hear you be stupid about it.

"What are you?"

[Unknown.]

"Who's doing this?"

[Unknown.]

"Do you know where I am?"

[Confirmed.]

You wait for the rest of it. There is no rest of it. Somewhere aft, very faintly, something that has not moved in a long time moves - and the page behind your eyes does not remark on that either.

OPTIONS:
1. Steps through the cut into the corridor || I go through before I can talk myself out of it, cutter still hot in my hand, and let the warm dark take the weight of the first step.
2. Welds the bulkhead shut and walks away || I put the cutter back to the seam and close it, badly and fast, and tell myself that eleven years of not knowing was survivable enough.
3. Keeps asking until it says something that is not [Unknown.] || I stay where I am and keep putting questions to it, one after another, until either it gives me something with content in it or I run out of ways to ask.

character_creation.label: Trade
character_creation.prompt: Eleven years of keeping this ship alive taught you one thing properly. The System will want to know which.

options.name: Coil-hand
options.tagline: You know the drive. You have had it apart on the hold floor more times than you have had a hot meal, and you got more of it lit than anyone would believe - but you have never once heard the ship, and you did not know there was anything to hear.

options.name: Listener
options.tagline: You run the arrays. You have been hearing something under the carrier for years and calling it a fault, and you have been half-right for so long it has worn a groove. The ship talks to you. It will not move.

options.name: Patcher
options.tagline: You keep the hull between you and the belt, and that is the whole of it. Nothing aboard is elegant and nothing aboard has killed you yet. You understand none of what is behind that bulkhead and you are the likeliest of anyone to survive finding out.

character_creation.label: Before the Garland
character_creation.prompt: Nobody chooses the Garland first. What put you here?

options.name: A debt somebody else made
options.tagline: It is still accruing, and the people holding it know exactly which belt you are working.

options.name: A warrant in a system you will not name
options.tagline: Old, quiet, and still open. The Garland's appeal was that nobody here asks.

options.name: A crew that did not come back
options.tagline: You were not aboard. You have never worked with anybody since, and you tell yourself that is practicality.
